item.title: Lahore ranked as the most polluted city in the world, again. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Lahore has once again emerged as the most polluted city in the world, with its air quality classified as “unhealthy”, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir, as Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the government was making efforts to address environmental issues.

In the past few years, air pollution has become one of the most pressing public health and environmental crises facing Pakistan. Various cities of the country, most notably Lahore, deal with smog, especially in the winter months. The phenomenon is attributed mainly to industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, stubble burning and air movement.

Lahore topped the list of the most polluted cities on Friday morning, with an air quality index (AQI) of 167, according to the IQAir live tracker, falling under the ‘unhealthy’ category, closely followed by Bangladesh’s Dhaka at 164 and Egypt’s Cairo at 158.

Later in the day, Lahore’s ranking in the list of the world’s most polluted cities dropped to 10th, with an AQI of 149 at 2:00pm.

The provincial capital was the only Pakistani city ranking in the top 30 most polluted cities on Friday morning. The only other Pakistani city in the 125-city list was Karachi at 34th place with an AQI of 69, on Friday morning.

Later in the day, Karachi moved up a few spots to number 23 with an AQI of 75, as of 2:00pm.

According to IQAir, in Lahore, “PM2.5 concentration is currently 15.2 times the World Health Organisation annual PM2.5 guideline value”.

PM2.5 refers to fine inhalable particles, with diameters generally 2.5 micrometres and smaller. Of all air pollution measures, PM2.5 pollution poses the greatest health threat, according to IQAir.

According to the website, PM2.5 can enter the circulatory system and even the brain, causing serious health complications if long-term exposure occurs.

For those in Lahore, IQAir recommended avoiding outdoor exercise, closing windows to avoid outdoor air, wearing a mask outdoors and installing an air purifier indoors.

Meanwhile, in a televised address to senior officers in Lahore on Friday, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the provincial government was making efforts to address environmental issues.

For the past eight years, she said, Lahore as well as some parts of Punjab would undergo a “smog shutdown” in September and October

“For three years now — I won’t say there is zero smog, but — there is less smog,” she said.

In January this year, Lahore was ranked as the most polluted city globally by IQAir with an AQI of 452. Earlier this week, a new analysis released by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) ranked Lahore among cities whose ozone levels were “extremely poor”.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with Australia. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent diplomatic engagement with the Australian High Commission could help move our relationship beyond traditional development aid toward a more ambitious, economic-first alliance.
As Bangladesh navigates a critical economic transition, deepening ties with a nation such as Australia across energy security, trade diversification, and technical education is the sort of partnership that could help us with our ambitions for sustainable growth.
At the heart of this evolving relationship is the shared imperative of energy security. As Bangladesh works to power its industrial capacity and meet expanding domestic demand, securing reliable liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports and attracting foreign direct investment in renewable energy, energy exploration, and grid logistics are certainly essential.
Australia, with its vast energy resources, green technology leadership, and expertise in resource management, is a perfect fit to support our transition toward a more resilient and diversified energy matrix.
Equally promising is the focus on human capital development. Expanding pathways for skilled professional migration in engineering, healthcare, and information technology creates valuable opportunities for Bangladeshi talent while helping fill key labour demands in Australia.
Proposals to link Bangladesh’s technical training centres with Australian vocational institutions, alongside efforts to bring offshore university campuses to Dhaka, reflect forward-thinking vision for development. Aligning local skill training with international technical standards is the sort of initiative we need to see to ensure that our youth can learn to compete successfully in the global economy.
Strengthening Bangladesh-Australia cooperation in areas of mutual interest could be crucial for our ongoing economic transformation. This is a partnership that promises long-term stability and mutual prosperity, and we must ensure that we are ready to take this relationship to the next level.

item.title: Getting tougher on public accountability. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The forced resignation of a sitting lawmaker and the dissolution of local party committees following multiple land grabbing incidents and attempts potentially mark a critical turning point for political governance.
It goes without saying that when public representatives and grassroots operatives become implicated in acts of mob violence, land grabbing, and criminal sabotage, the integrity of the entire political system is compromised.
While organizational dismissals and parliamentary resignations are necessary first steps, and we commend the state for taking swift action, we must go far further to systematically excise bad actors from public life.
Political affiliation in Bangladesh has long functioned as a shield against legal accountability. Local leaders, clout-chasers, and organized muscle have routinely exploited political patronage to seize property, intimidate communities, and subvert laws with complete impunity.
Our law enforcement too is not above criticism; at a time when we have needed them to be proactive and assist with dismantling criminal activities, their passivity has only emboldened criminal behaviour.
What we have is a deep-seated culture of impunity that continues to undermine the rule of law, and it is one that we must eliminate.
Internal party discipline, while commendable, cannot replace state justice. Forcing rogue actors to step down or stripping them of party membership addresses the political optics, but it does not satisfy the demands of the law.
As such, criminal acts must be met with rigorous investigation, transparent prosecution, and severe judicial penalties, regardless of an individual's standing or political ties.
If our country is to break free from the destructive cycles of political hooliganism, we must expect better from our political leaders. The message must be clear: Extortionists and land grabbers have no place here.
